extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in mathematics / applied mathematics interested in PDE theory and methods
extracted.subtask_description: A rapid, broad survey of modern partial differential equations (PDEs) covering major equation types, typical behaviors, core theoretical goals (existence/uniqueness/continuous dependence), and principal analytic, variational and numerical methods used to study them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three primary mathematical approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: There are at least three primary mathematical approaches to understanding PDEs: discovering analytical formulas for solutions (exact or approximate), devising accurate and fast numerical methods, and developing rigorous theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose among (or combine) explicit solution construction, numerical computation, and rigorous theoretical analysis depending on the equation and goal; the article emphasizes rigorous theory but notes the complementary roles of formulas and numerics.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDE classification: order, system, linearity
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology: PDE order is the highest partial derivative order appearing; systems involve vector-valued unknowns; a PDE is linear if it corresponds to a linear operator acting on the unknown and its partial derivatives, otherwise it is nonlinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the PDE early (order, scalar vs system, linear vs nonlinear) as this shapes applicable techniques and expected phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary and initial conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most PDEs are studied subject to appropriate boundary and/or initial conditions; e.g. Dirichlet condition (u = g on ∂U) and Neumann condition (∂u/∂ν = 0 on ∂U), and initial data u(·,0)=g (and ut(·,0)=h for second-order-in-time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe boundary/initial data suitable to physical interpretation (temperature, flux, etc.). The choice of conditions is essential to make problems well-posed and to select correct solution notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact solutions and explicit formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, solve the PDE explicitly (Poisson's formula, d'Alembert, Kirchhoff, heat kernel). Some nonlinear PDEs (e.g. KdV) are exactly solvable (integrable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit formulas where available to obtain quantitative insight; but note the fundamental truth that most PDEs cannot be solved explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate solutions and perturbation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct systematic perturbation schemes when PDEs depend on a small parameter: posit corrections and tune to make error small. Techniques include multiple scales and asymptotic matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use homogenization/multiple-scale expansions to derive effective PDEs; apply asymptotic matching (outer/inner expansions) to handle boundary layers and determine scalings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical analysis and method selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Devising effective computer algorithms (finite difference, method of lines, finite element, spectral, multigrid, level set, etc.) is a vast enterprise; design and analysis of numerical methods depend on good theoretical understanding of the PDE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select numerical schemes tailored to equation type (conservation laws, diffusion, waves) and informed by stability, consistency, error estimates, and PDE-specific structure (e.g., conservation, shocks, stiff layers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory and the importance of analytic estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous theory focuses on existence, smoothness, and uniqueness; deriving 'hard' analytic estimates is central, and theorists couple these with 'soft' tools to exploit estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a priori estimates (energy, entropy, monotonicity, etc.) as foundational steps toward well-posedness and regularity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-posedness (existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-posed PDE problem means (a) the solution exists, (b) is unique, and (c) depends continuously on the given data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish well-posedness as the starting point for further analysis, numerical methods, and approximate solution construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized solution notions
rubrics_metrics.description: For many PDEs one must adopt generalized notions of solution: distributional solutions for linear PDEs; for nonlinear problems notions include viscosity solutions, entropy solutions, renormalized solutions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the notion of generalized solution appropriate to the PDE and phenomena (e.g., entropy solutions for conservation laws with shocks; viscosity solutions for Hamilton–Jacobi equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy methods and functional-analytic framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Use integral 'energy' expressions (often involving squared quantities) and integration by parts to derive conservation or dissipation identities; energy estimates are used to control solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute energies (e.g., wave energy e(t)=∫(ut^2 + c^2|∇u|^2)/2 dx) and show conservation or decay; use integration by parts and Sobolev-space techniques to obtain a priori bounds and regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts and divergence theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration by parts (a form of the Divergence Theorem) is a central tool: ∫_U u_xi v = −∫_U u v_xi + ∫_{∂U} u v ν_i dS, used to move derivatives between functions in energy/variational calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply carefully with boundary/decay assumptions; justifies derivation of Euler–Lagrange equations and energy identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy estimates (elliptic and time-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy identities and inequalities (e.g., conservation for wave equation, modified energies for nonlinear waves) yield control over solution norms and sometimes imply regularity (e.g., from ∆u square-integrable to uxixj square-integrable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit energy identities to deduce integrability/smoothness of derivatives and to obtain uniqueness/stability results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variational formulation and Euler–Lagrange equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if a PDE is variational: u minimizes I[u]=∫_U L(∇u,u,x) dx, then first variation yields Euler–Lagrange: −div(∇_v L(∇u,u,x)) + L_z(∇u,u,x)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variational structure to obtain existence (direct method), regularity, and to connect PDEs to geometry (minimal surfaces) and physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointwise maximum principle techniques: if u attains interior maximum then gradient zero and Hessian negative semidefinite; for linear elliptic Lu=0 with c>0, u cannot attain a positive interior maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply maximum principles to deduce uniqueness, bounds, and qualitative behavior for elliptic and certain nonlinear equations (e.g., Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform methods (Fourier, Laplace, Fourier series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integral transforms convert linear constant-coefficient PDEs into algebraic equations (Fourier transform, Laplace transform in time, Fourier series on bounded domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transforms to solve or represent solutions (e.g., solve −∆u+u=f via (1+|y|^2)û=ƒ̂ and invert), and to derive fundamental solutions and kernels (heat kernel formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential inequalities and monotonicity formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Design integral expressions (often over balls) that satisfy differential inequalities in a remaining variable to derive monotonicity or scale-invariant control (example: monotonicity for harmonic-map-type integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monotonicity to deduce fine-scale behavior from larger scales, useful in regularity and blow-up analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissipation and gradient-flow estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: For gradient flows ut − div(∇L(∇u)) = 0 one can define energies e(t)=∫ L(∇u)/2 and show ˙e(t)=−∫ (ut)^2 ≤ 0, demonstrating dissipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dissipation identities to show convergence, decay, and to control long-time behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy estimates for conservation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: For viscous conservation laws with small viscosity, convex entropy Φ and associated flux Ψ produce dissipation inequalities ˙e(t)=−∫( (ε Φ''(u)(u_x)^2 ) + boundary_terms ) ≤ 0, yielding many dissipation inequalities corresponding to entropy/entropy-flux pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find entropy/entropy-flux pairs to obtain stability and compactness needed for existence and uniqueness of entropy solutions; this is a major challenge for systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity theory and higher integrability
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity theory aims to deduce higher integrability/smoothness of solutions from available estimates (e.g., if ∆u ∈ L^2 then second derivatives uxixj ∈ L^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine energy estimates, elliptic theory, and functional-analytic tools to upgrade weak solutions to stronger regularity where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and examples of key PDEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Important PDE examples include: scalar conservation law ut+div F(u)=0; Hamilton–Jacobi ut+H(∇u,x)=0; Laplace ∆u=0; heat ut−∆u=0; wave utt−c^2∆u=0; Schrödinger iut+∆u=0; Euler and Navier–Stokes for fluids; reaction–diffusion ut−∆u=f(u); Maxwell's equations; KdV ut+auux+buxxx=0; biharmonic ∆^2 u=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific structure of these canonical equations to select analytic and numerical methods, and to understand typical behaviors (dispersion, diffusion, shocks, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave phenomena: traveling waves, plane waves, dispersion, solitons
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for structured solutions: traveling waves u(x,t)=v(x−σt), plane waves u(x,t)=v(y·x−σt), and complex plane waves u=e^{i(y·x−σt)} to derive dispersion relations; nonlinear examples yield solitons (e.g., KdV sech^2 profile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching for special structured solutions is a useful first step to understand propagation, speeds, and nonlinear coherent structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion and instantaneous smoothing
rubrics_metrics.description: The heat equation smooths initial data: if initial data g is merely integrable then solution u(x,t) becomes infinitely differentiable for t>0 (instantaneous smoothing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit explicit kernels (heat kernel) to deduce regularization and decay properties; contrast with wave equations where smoothing differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation speed: finite vs infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Different PDEs exhibit different propagation phenomena: heat equation has infinite propagation speed (initial data everywhere influences u(x,t) for t>0), while many PDEs (first-order, wave equation, some nonlinear diffusions like porous medium for γ>1) have finite propagation speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize propagation properties to set expectations for influence domains, causality, and support evolution (e.g., porous medium explicit solution shows finite-speed positivity spread).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern formation and geometric motion of interfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Reaction–diffusion systems with multistable potentials (e.g., two-well Φ) can produce patterns where regions approach minima ±1 and interfaces Γ(t) move by geometric laws (normal velocity equals curvature in certain asymptotic limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use asymptotic matching and modulation arguments to derive reduced geometric laws describing interface motion in singular-perturbation limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions of time-dependent PDEs may blow up in finite time (e.g., spatially constant solutions of ut−∆u=u^2 reduce to ODE ut=u^2 that blows up), reflecting competition between stabilizing diffusion and destabilizing nonlinearities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze energy/maximum-principle and comparison arguments to identify blow-up mechanisms and to estimate blow-up times and profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shocks and discontinuities in conservation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservation laws can develop discontinuities (shocks) even from smooth initial data due to characteristic crossing (e.g., Burgers' equation); theory must characterize shock surfaces for generalized (entropy) solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop entropy conditions, weak formulations, and jump conditions to select physically relevant solutions and to analyze existence/uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free boundary problems and obstacle problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some problems require finding both the solution and the region where the PDE holds (Stefan problem for phase change; obstacle problem min{u, −∆u − f}=0 with free boundary Γ=∂{u>0}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat free-boundary problems by coupling PDE analysis with geometric/topological arguments; variational formulations and monotonicity formulas are often pivotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrable nonlinear PDEs and their special role
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain nonlinear PDEs (e.g., KdV) are integrable and exactly solvable, producing solitons and rich structure; discovering integrable PDEs is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When integrability is present, use inverse scattering and related explicit tools; otherwise pursue approximate/numerical/theoretical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between theoretical analysis and numerical design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and analysis of numerical methods (especially for nonlinear equations) depends upon a good theoretical understanding of the underlying PDE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PDE estimates (stability, entropy, energy) to guide discretization choices, ensure convergence, and capture essential phenomena like shocks or interface motion.
